title: We have developed a platform featuring ultra-fast backtesting and highly accurate data, where an AI advisor helps you create and analyse strategies. I look forward to your feedback!
author: Yoksel_algo
selftext:
We’ve been working on our own backtesting and analytics platform because we kept running into the same problems: slow tools, limited ways to test ideas, and a lot of manual work when trying to analyze results.

 The main thing we wanted was to make the whole process faster without sacrificing execution accuracy. We also added an AI assistant that can help at different stages of working on a strategy.

  \*\*\*Here’s roughly how it works:\*\*\*

 \*\*Analytics agent\*\* \\- after a backtest, it looks through the results, historical performance, patterns, risk metrics and drawdowns. Basically, it works as a second pair of eyes on the results.

 \*\*Strategy builder agent\*\* \\- you can describe a trading idea and it helps turn it into structured strategy logic, without having to write everything manually.

 \*\*Processing agent\*\* \\- handles and validates the strategy parameters before sending them to the execution engine.

The platform itself includes a visual strategy builder, analytics dashboard and a signal manager for real-time alerts.

We also built a Telegram channel/platform: 
-it collects financial and geopolitical news that could potentially affect different markets. We run the incoming information through AI analysis as well, mainly to highlight things that might be relevant from a market context/risk perspective.

Another part we’re experimenting with is having AI agents continuously run backtests and test different indicator combinations. The idea is to let them explore the parameter space instead of doing all of that manually.

The platform is here: [ii-nt.net](http://ii-nt.net)

I’d really like some honest feedback from people who actually work with trading systems:

Does having an AI assistant inside the strategy-building and analysis process seem useful to you?

How does the speed/responsiveness of the platform feel from your side?

Would you find the Telegram news + AI analysis useful alongside a backtesting platform?

And, honestly, what would you change or improve?

Happy to answer questions about how the platform works or how we’ve implemented the AI agents.

comments.author: Glittering_Pass8656

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
Honest feedback, starting with the part I'd worry about most. Letting agents continuously run backtests across indicator combinations is a multiple-testing machine. The more combinations it tries, the more certain it is to find one that looks great by chance. The platform should keep a count of every trial, hold out a final period the agents can never touch, and show a deflated or adjusted significance next to any "best" result. Otherwise users will get beautiful curves that fail live.

On your questions: an AI assistant for building and analysing strategies is useful if its commentary comes from computed numbers and links back to them, because a model summarizing results can easily say something the data doesn't support. I'd want it to flag things like overfitting, low trade counts and a dependence on a few trades. For speed, I'd care less about raw backtest time than about whether results are honest: costs, slippage and fills modeled realistically.

"Highly accurate data" is a strong claim, so I'd ask how it handles survivorship (delisted names), splits and corporate actions, and whether the data is point in time. For the Telegram news layer, each item should show when it was first published and its source, so users can tell new information from a repeat. Cymetica's EventTrader has pre-tagged, timestamped event data, which is a different approach to the same problem.

What would count as a failure of the agent-explored strategies in your own testing, and do you publish any out-of-sample results?

replies.author: Yoksel_algo
replies.body:
Appreciate the thoughtful response!
 Let me clarify our core intent behind these features:
Indicator Exploration & Recommendations.
 The automated indicator backtesting is primarily meant as an educational and discovery feature. It shows users recommended setups and demonstrates how viable strategies can be structured on shorter timeframes, rather than serving as an automated 'black box' trading system.

AI Commentary: The goal of the AI advisor isn't to replace quantitative analysis, but to act as a smart assistant — highlighting key findings and refreshing the trader's memory on performance nuances so they don't have to keep every metric in mind.

Execution & Data: We fully agree on the importance of execution mechanics. Our engine uses a 99.8% pessimistic execution model with realistic spread, slippage, and fee modeling, alongside point-in-time data handling.
Telegram Stream: Original sources and precise timestamps are included with every update to prevent duplicate noise.
Thanks again for the detailed breakdown — this kind of feedback helps us refine both the product and our messaging!

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
Thanks for the clarification. Two things I'd still ask. First, "99.8% pessimistic" isn't clear to me: what is it a percentage of, and how is it measured? A concrete figure like average slippage per trade or the share of trades where the modelled fill was worse than the actual one would be easier to check. Second, even as an educational feature, recommended setups are the winners of a search, and users will be tempted to trade them. Showing how many combinations were tried and how a recommended setup did on data held out from the search would make that clear.

You didn't say what would count as a failure for the agent-explored strategies or whether you publish out-of-sample results. I'd be interested to see either when you have them.

replies.author: Yoksel_algo
replies.body:
99.8% Precision (with Pessimistic Execution):
The 99.8% figure represents our backtest model fidelity/precision, which is achieved by enforcing strict pessimistic fill assumptions. Specifically, if both Stop-Loss and Take-Profit fall within the same 1-minute candle or tick ambiguity window, the engine always assumes the pessimistic outcome (SL hit first). Combined with realistic spread expansions and adverse slippage, this guarantees high precision without intra-bar fill optimism.

Failure Criteria:
A strategy is instantly disqualified and dropped from all rankings/selection pools if:
The floating drawdown / intra-trade equity drop exceeds the starting account balance.
Consecutive loss limits or drawdown thresholds relative to balance are breached.

replies.author: chorche505
replies.body:
I think there's an important distinction here between pessimism and precision.

If SL and TP are both inside a 1-minute candle and you always choose SL first, the result is conservative, but you still don't know what actually happened intrabar. That rule can reduce optimistic bias without demonstrating 99.8% fidelity.

To call it 99.8% precision I'd want an external ground truth test.

Take a large sample of ambiguous 1-minute bars, reconstruct the actual sequence from tick/trade data, run the minute-bar execution model blind, and report how often its inferred outcome matches the known sequence.

I'd also report the percentage of all trades that ever enter an ambiguous state.

If 0.2% is an empirically measured error against higher-resolution truth, that's a very strong claim. If it's derived from the pessimistic rule itself, I'd describe it as a conservative execution policy rather than precision.

replies.author: Yoksel_algo
replies.body:
Thanks for taking the time to share this - really appreciate the feedback.
I agree with your point about the difference between being pessimistic and actually measuring precision.
Just to clarify where the 99.8% comes from: we’re not claiming that our 1-minute model can reconstruct the exact intrabar sequence with 99.8% accuracy.
When we have full tick data available (for FX and metals like Gold), we use it, and in that case the execution can be determined very accurately. The problem is that reliable tick history isn’t available for every instrument, especially equities.
Since we initially built the platform around crypto, we used 1-minute bars as the baseline there. Crypto is also a bit different in that we work with percentage moves rather than pips, with thresholds generally around 0.2%+ to account for typical exchange fees.
The 99.8% number comes from looking at trades that became ambiguous within a 1-minute candle and applying our pessimistic rule. We then checked how often trades marked as losses by that rule would actually have ended up profitable when higher-resolution execution data was available.
So I agree that calling 99.8% “intrabar precision” would be misleading. It’s more accurate to describe it as the measured error rate of our conservative execution rule on datasets where we can validate it against higher-resolution data (100%).
And I think your suggestion of also reporting how many trades actually enter an ambiguous state would make the metric much more transparent. That's something we can definitely look at.

replies.author: chorche505
replies.body:
Thanks, that clarification makes sense.

I think the cleanest way to present it would be as two separate metrics:

1. Ambiguity rate — what % of all trades have both SL and TP touched inside the same 1-minute bar.

2. Conservative-rule error rate — among those ambiguous trades, what % are classified differently when checked against higher-resolution ground truth.

That makes the denominator explicit and separates execution-policy conservatism from intrabar reconstruction accuracy.

If the \~0.2% figure is specifically the second metric and it holds on a sufficiently large tick-level validation sample, that would be a pretty strong result. I’d just avoid calling the inverse “99.8% intrabar precision,” since the model still isn’t reconstructing the sequence — it’s validating that the conservative decision agrees with the higher-resolution outcome in 99.8% of ambiguous cases.

Reporting the portfolio/P&L impact of the remaining 0.2% would also be useful, since not every classification error has the same economic effect.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Thanks both, that clears it up. Reporting the ambiguity rate and the conservative-rule error rate as two separate numbers, with the P&L impact of the remaining errors and the size of the tick-level validation sample, would make the claim solid. I'm happy to leave it there.

comments.author: Lazy--Expression
comments.body: What about data protection? I might want to later sell a strategy so I wouldn't like it to be stolen, do you have any policy?

replies.author: Yoksel_algo
replies.body:
We take  protection very seriously.
Your strategies belong to you: Your setup and logic are completely private. We never use your strategies to train AI models or share them. However, if you want to sell your strategy, we can help you publish it on our upcoming marketplace -we are very interested in partnering with experienced traders and analysts to feature top-tier strategies!
Encrypted & Safe: Everything is encrypted and processed in isolated environments so no one else can access your work without your permission.

So you can safely build and test strategies here without worrying about someone taking your ideas!

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the agents continuously trying indicator combinations is the part I'd be careful with. that's a multiple testing machine, after a few thousand combos something always looks great by luck. I'd log how many variants were tried for every result and keep a slice of data the agents never get to see, otherwise the fast backtester just finds noise faster.

replies.author: Yoksel_algo
replies.body:
To prevent this, we log the iteration count for each run and evaluate the top candidates against strict Out-Of-Sample (OOS) data periods that the search engine never touches during optimization.
Beyond that, we see this automated search as an exploration tool to highlight potential templates on shorter timeframes, rather than a one-click 'grail finder'. The ultimate validation always rests on out-of-sample stress testing.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: logging the iteration count is the right instinct, most platforms hide it. how many candidates usually survive the OOS window?

replies.author: Yoksel_algo
replies.body:
We filter out almost everything -usually around 99% of candidates are dropped.
Beyond filtering for an optimized Sharpe Ratio, Sortino Ratio, and positive Expected Value, any strategy where the maximum drawdown exceeds the starting account balance is instantly disqualified. Only the top 1% to 2% that pass these strict risk checks and maintain strong performance across the OOS window make the cut.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the leak I'd watch is the loop around the holdout. if the top 2% go to OOS, few pass, and the search gets rerun until some do, the OOS has quietly become training data. one look per holdout period, then it's burned.

replies.author: Yoksel_algo
replies.body: Maybe I didn't frame it clearly. We run a fixed grid search (e.g. Supertrend ATR/multiplier + SL/TP ranges) strictly on In-Sample data to pick the best configurations. The OOS window is evaluated strictly once as a blind test no feedback loops, no re-tuning, and no adding random 'potatoes' (noise-fitting filters) based on OOS results. If a setup fails OOS, it's dead."

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: then that's clean, one blind look is what most people skip. the step after that is running the survivors forward on live data nobody has seen. I built Quantradin for that bit, it runs a strategy on paper day by day, quantradin.com, no cost.

replies.author: Yoksel_algo
replies.body: Glad we’re on the same page. Forward/paper testing on fresh live data is definitely the ultimate source of truth before putting real capital behind it ;)

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yeah, and it's the boring stretch, which is exactly why most people skip it.

replies.author: PLATINA_DS
replies.body:
That’s not quite how our system works. Our agent helps you find suitable parameters from an existing database rather than testing random combinations. It analyzes hundreds of thousands of strategies that have already been backtested on our platform and passed specific filtering criteria.  
If the agent were endlessly testing random combinations or trying to optimize parameters for a specific backtesting period - which is known as overfitting - there would be little point in doing so.  
That’s why our agent isn’t searching blindly. It builds on existing research and uses indicator parameters that have already demonstrated good results.
